goals: Draw and label a vertical section of the eye and state the function of each part
Explain how the ciliary muscles change the lens for near and distant vision
Explain adaptation to light and dark and the advantage of stereoscopic vision

slides.heading: Sense Organs: Eye and Ear
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the eye, a living camera.

visual.alt: Flow: light from an object is focused by the cornea and lens onto the retina, and the optic nerve carries impulses to the brain

slides.narration: The eye works much like a camera. The cornea and lens focus light onto the retina, which acts like the film. Rods and cones turn the light into nerve impulses, and the brain turns these into the picture we see.

slides.heading: Inside the eye
slides.body_md: The wall has three layers: **sclera**, **choroid** and **retina**. In front are the **cornea**, **iris** and **lens**.

slides.narration: The tough white sclera bulges at the front as the clear cornea. Inside it the dark choroid carries blood vessels. The innermost layer, the retina, holds the light-sensitive cells. The lens hangs from the ciliary body by suspensory ligaments.

slides.heading: Parts of the eye and their functions

rows: Thin membrane protecting the front of the eye
Transparent; lets light in and bends it
Iris controls the size of the pupil, so the light entering
Its muscles change the curvature of the lens
Keep the eyeball in shape; let light through
Dark, with blood vessels; absorbs stray light
Rods and cones turn light into impulses

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the eye and their functions

slides.narration: Follow the light. It passes the conjunctiva and cornea, the watery aqueous humour, the pupil and the lens, then the jelly-like vitreous humour, and lands on the retina. The dark choroid stops light bouncing around inside.

slides.heading: Quick check: the front window
slides.body_md: Name the transparent, bulging front part of the eye.
slides.narration: It is the part replaced in eye donation.

slides.heading: The retina: rods, cones and two special spots

rows: Work in dim light; no colour; contain visual purple (needs vitamin A)
Work in bright light; give colour vision
Where the optic nerve leaves: no rods or cones, no image

visual.alt: Table of rods, cones, the yellow spot and the blind spot

slides.narration: The retina has two kinds of light-sensitive cells. Rods help us see in dim light. Cones give us colour and detail. Vision is sharpest at the yellow spot, and we see nothing at the blind spot, where the optic nerve leaves.

slides.heading: Quick check: the sharpest spot
slides.body_md: True or false: cones are most closely packed at the yellow spot.
slides.narration: Where is vision clearest?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: finding your blind spot
slides.body_md: Draw a cross and, a hand's width to its right, a dot. Close your left eye and look at the cross with your right eye.
bullets: Step 1: hold the card at arm's length and keep staring at the cross.
Step 2: bring the card slowly towards your face.
Step 3: at one distance the dot vanishes: its image has fallen on the blind spot.

rows: Its image falls on rods and cones
Image falls on the blind spot: no receptors
Dot reappears when the card moves on
Image moves off the blind spot

visual.alt: Worked table of observations in the blind-spot test and their explanations

slides.narration: Try it. As the card comes closer, the dot suddenly disappears and then comes back. At that moment its image lies on the blind spot, where there are no rods or cones. We do not normally notice the gap because our two eyes cover for each other.

slides.body_md: Near object: **ciliary muscles contract**, ligaments slacken, lens **thicker**. Distant object: muscles **relax**, ligaments tight, lens **thinner**.

slides.narration: The eye focuses by changing the shape of its lens. To look at something near, the ciliary muscles contract, the ligaments loosen and the elastic lens bulges. For distant objects the muscles relax and the lens is pulled flat. This is accommodation.

slides.narration: The iris works like a camera's aperture. In bright light it narrows the pupil to protect the retina. In dim light it opens the pupil wide. Inside the rods, visual purple is bleached by bright light and slowly rebuilt in the dark.

slides.heading: Light and dark adaptation

visual.alt: Table comparing the eye in bright light and in dim light

slides.narration: Walking into a dark room, you see little at first because the pupil takes time to widen and the visual purple must be rebuilt. Walking out into sunlight dazzles you until the pupil narrows.

slides.heading: Stereoscopic vision
slides.body_md: Our eyes face forward, so their fields of view **overlap**: both eyes see the same scene from slightly different angles.

slides.narration: Each eye sees the scene from a slightly different angle. The brain combines the two views into one picture with depth. This is stereoscopic vision, and it lets us judge how far away things are.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how much do the fields overlap?
slides.body_md: Each eye sees about **150°**; together they see about **180°**.
bullets: Step 1: add the two fields: 150 + 150 = 300°.
Step 2: the total seen is only 180°, so the extra is counted twice.
Step 3: overlap = 300 − 180 = **120°**, seen by both eyes.

visual.alt: Worked table: one eye one hundred and fifty degrees, both together one hundred and eighty, overlap one hundred and twenty

slides.narration: Add the two fields and take away the total. The part counted twice is the overlap, about one hundred and twenty degrees in front of us. Animals that hunt have a large overlap; animals that are hunted, like rabbits, have eyes on the sides and very little.

slides.heading: Quick check: two eyes
slides.body_md: Stereoscopic vision mainly helps us to…
slides.narration: Think of threading a needle.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Wall: sclera (cornea in front), choroid, retina.
Iris controls the pupil; lens focuses; ciliary body changes the lens.
Rods: dim light. Cones: bright light, colour. Yellow spot: sharpest. Blind spot: no image.
Accommodation: near, lens thicker; far, lens thinner.
Stereoscopic vision: about 120° of overlap lets us judge depth.

visual.alt: Summary table of the ciliary muscles and the lens for near and distant objects

slides.narration: To recap. Light passes through the cornea, pupil and lens onto the retina. The ciliary muscles adjust the lens for near and far. The iris adjusts the pupil for bright and dim light. And two forward-facing eyes give us depth.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Near vision: ciliary muscles **contract**, lens **thicker**.
Bright light: **circular** muscles; dim light: **radial** muscles.
Yellow spot = **most cones**; blind spot = **none**.
In eye diagrams, label all **three coats** and both **humours**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Get the ciliary muscles right: they contract for near objects. Match circular muscles with bright light. Do not confuse the yellow spot with the blind spot. And label every layer in your eye diagram.

slides.narration: Many of us wear spectacles. In this part we see why: what goes wrong in common eye defects and how lenses fix them. Then we turn to the ear, which does two jobs: hearing, and keeping us balanced.

slides.heading: Five eye defects

rows: Eyeball too long or lens too curved; image in front of retina
Eyeball too short or lens too flat; image behind retina
Lens less elastic with age; near objects blurred

visual.alt: Table of five eye defects with their causes and corrections

slides.narration: Myopia and hypermetropia come from an eyeball of the wrong length. Presbyopia comes with age, as the lens stiffens. Astigmatism comes from an unevenly curved cornea. And in cataract the lens turns cloudy and must be replaced.

slides.body_md: Distant objects blurred: rays meet **in front of** the retina. A **concave** lens corrects it.

slides.narration: The pinna funnels sound into the auditory canal to the ear drum. Behind it, in the air-filled middle ear, three tiny bones form a chain. The inner ear holds the coiled cochlea for hearing, and the vestibule and semicircular canals for balance.

rows: Leads sound to the ear drum; wax traps dust
Joins middle ear to throat; equalises air pressure

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the ear and their functions

slides.narration: Each part has one main job. The ossicles are the smallest bones in the body. The Eustachian tube keeps the air pressure the same on both sides of the ear drum, which is why swallowing helps when your ears feel blocked in a plane.

slides.heading: How we hear

nodes.label: Oval window; fluid of the cochlea

visual.alt: Flow of sound from the pinna to the brain

slides.narration: Sound waves set the ear drum vibrating. The three ossicles pass the vibrations to the oval window and make the fluid in the cochlea move. Sensory hair cells change this movement into nerve impulses, and the brain recognises them as sound.

slides.heading: How the ear keeps us balanced

Position of the head with respect to gravity

visual.alt: Table of the semicircular canals and vestibule in balance

slides.narration: The three semicircular canals lie at right angles, so turning in any direction moves the fluid in at least one of them. The vestibule senses which way is down. The brain uses both to keep us upright.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: why we feel dizzy
slides.body_md: Follow the fluid in the semicircular canals during and after a spin.
bullets: Step 1: as you start spinning, the fluid lags behind and bends the sensory hairs: the brain senses turning.
Step 2: when you stop suddenly, the fluid keeps moving for a while.
Step 3: the hairs still signal turning, though you are still: you feel **dizzy**.

visual.alt: Worked table of the fluid in the semicircular canals and the feeling at the start, during and after a spin

slides.narration: The fluid in the canals behaves like tea in a cup you turn. When you stop, it keeps swirling. Your eyes say you are still, but your canals say you are turning, and the mismatch makes you dizzy.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Myopia: concave lens. Hypermetropia and presbyopia: convex lens. Astigmatism: cylindrical lens. Cataract: surgery.
Ear: outer (pinna, canal), middle (tympanum, ossicles, Eustachian tube), inner (cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals).
Hearing: tympanum → ossicles → cochlea → auditory nerve → brain.
Balance: semicircular canals for movement, vestibule for position.

visual.alt: Summary table: the cochlea is for hearing; the semicircular canals and vestibule are for balance

slides.narration: To recap. The length of the eyeball decides whether you are short or long sighted, and the right lens corrects it. The ear passes vibrations from the ear drum to the cochlea for hearing, and uses separate canals to keep you balanced.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Ray diagrams are needed **only** for myopia and hypermetropia.
Myopia: image **in front of** retina, **concave** lens. Hypermetropia: **behind**, **convex**.
Name the ossicles **in order**: malleus, incus, stapes.
Cochlea = hearing; semicircular canals and vestibule = balance.

sections.heading: 1. Structure of the eye
sections.body_md:
**External:** the eyeball sits in the bony **orbit**; eyelids, eyelashes and the **conjunctiva** (a thin transparent membrane over the front) protect it.

**Three coats:**
- **Sclera** — tough, white outer coat; in front it bulges as the transparent **cornea**, which lets light in and bends it.
- **Choroid** — dark, with blood vessels; nourishes the retina and **absorbs stray light**. In front it forms the **ciliary body** (with ciliary muscles) and the **iris**, which controls the size of the **pupil**.
- **Retina** — innermost, light-sensitive: **rods** (dim light, no colour; contain **visual purple**, made with vitamin A) and **cones** (bright light, colour). The **yellow spot** has the most cones (sharpest vision); the **blind spot**, where the **optic nerve** leaves, has none.

**Lens** — transparent, biconvex, elastic; held by **suspensory ligaments** from the ciliary body; focuses light on the retina.
**Aqueous humour** (between cornea and lens) and **vitreous humour** (jelly behind the lens) keep the shape of the eyeball.

sections.heading: 2. Accommodation, adaptation and stereoscopic vision
sections.body_md:
**Accommodation** — focusing on objects at different distances by changing the curvature of the lens.
- **Near object:** ciliary muscles **contract** → suspensory ligaments **slacken** → lens **thicker**, more convex (shorter focal length).
- **Distant object:** ciliary muscles **relax** → ligaments **tight** → lens **thinner**, flatter.

**Adaptation to light and dark:**
- **Bright light:** **circular** muscles of the iris contract → pupil **small**; visual purple in rods bleached; cones used.
- **Dim light:** **radial** muscles contract → pupil **large**; visual purple rebuilt (takes several minutes); rods used.

**Stereoscopic (binocular) vision:** both eyes face forward and their fields overlap (each about 150°, together about 180°, overlap about 120°). The brain fuses the two slightly different views into one **three-dimensional** image, so we can **judge depth and distance**.

key_terms.definition_md: Adjustment of the lens to focus near and distant objects.
Vision with two overlapping fields, giving depth.

sections.body_md:
| Defect | Cause | Effect | Correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Myopia** (short sight) | Eyeball too long or lens too curved | Distant objects blurred; image **in front of** retina | **Concave** lens |

| **Presbyopia** | Lens loses elasticity, ciliary muscles weaken with age | Near objects blurred | Convex or bifocal lens |
| **Astigmatism** | Uneven curvature of the cornea | Lines in some directions blurred | **Cylindrical** lens |
| **Cataract** | Lens becomes cloudy (opaque) | Blurred, dim vision | Surgery: artificial lens |

sections.heading: 4. Structure of the ear
sections.body_md:
- **Outer ear:** **pinna** (collects sound) and **auditory canal** (with hairs and wax glands that trap dust), ending at the **tympanum** (ear drum).
- **Middle ear:** an air-filled cavity with three **ossicles** — **malleus** (hammer), **incus** (anvil), **stapes** (stirrup; the smallest bone in the body) — joined in a chain from the tympanum to the **oval window**. The **Eustachian tube** connects it to the **throat** and equalises air pressure on both sides of the ear drum.
- **Inner ear** (membranous labyrinth with fluid): the coiled **cochlea**, containing the **organ of Corti** (hearing); the **vestibule** (utriculus and sacculus); three **semicircular canals** at right angles, each with a swelling (ampulla) holding sensory hairs. The **auditory nerve** runs to the brain.

sections.heading: 5. Hearing and balance
sections.body_md:
**Path of sound:** pinna → auditory canal → **tympanum** vibrates → **malleus → incus → stapes** (vibrations transmitted and amplified) → **oval window** → fluid in the **cochlea** → sensory hair cells of the **organ of Corti** produce impulses → **auditory nerve** → **brain** (cerebrum), where sound is perceived.

**Balance:**
- **Semicircular canals** detect **movement and rotation** (dynamic balance): turning the head moves the fluid, which bends sensory hairs.
- **Vestibule** detects the **position of the head** with respect to gravity (static balance).
- After spinning, the fluid keeps moving for a while, so we feel **dizzy**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the ciliary muscles relax for near vision: they **contract**.
- Swapping the iris muscles: **circular** for bright light, **radial** for dim light.
- Confusing the **yellow spot** (most cones) with the **blind spot** (none).
- Using a convex lens for myopia; drawing ray diagrams for defects other than myopia and hypermetropia.
- Putting balance in the cochlea.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term (cataract, accommodation), a part named, an odd one out **with its category**.
- 2 marks: two differences, a mechanism (accommodation, adaptation) in two steps.
- 3 marks: a labelled eye or ear, ray diagrams for myopia or hypermetropia, the path of sound.

questions.stem_md: The clear, jelly-like substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina and keeps the eyeball in shape is the
questions.solution_md: The vitreous humour fills the large chamber behind the lens — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In eye donation, the part most often transplanted to restore sight to a person with a scarred front of the eye is the
questions.solution_md: A damaged, cloudy cornea can be replaced by a donor cornea — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A diet poor in vitamin A causes night blindness because

options.text_md: the cones need vitamin A to see colours
the lens becomes cloudy without it
the pupil cannot narrow without it
the rods need vitamin A to make visual purple

questions.solution_md: Visual purple (rhodopsin) in the rods is made from vitamin A; without it, vision in dim light fails — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** No image is formed on the blind spot.

**Reason (R):** The blind spot has the largest number of cones in the retina.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: the blind spot has no rods or cones; the yellow spot has the most cones — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cones are most closely packed at the yellow spot of the retina.
questions.solution_md: True. The yellow spot (fovea) is crowded with cones, giving the sharpest vision.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the tough, white, outer coat of the eyeball.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sclera** (sclerotic layer).

questions.solution_md: Sclera.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the thin, transparent membrane that covers the front of the eyeball and lines the eyelids.

answer.model_answer_md: **Conjunctiva.**

questions.solution_md: Conjunctiva.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Cornea, Lens, Cochlea, Retina.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cochlea**; the others are **parts of the eye**.

questions.solution_md: The cochlea is part of the inner ear.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the choroid of the eye is dark in colour.

answer.model_answer_md: Its dark **pigment absorbs stray light**, preventing **reflection** inside the eye that would blur the image (its blood vessels also nourish the retina).

questions.solution_md: Absorbs stray light.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: an object whose image falls on the blind spot is not seen.

answer.model_answer_md: The blind spot has **no rods or cones**, so no impulse is sent to the brain.

questions.solution_md: No receptors.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between rods and cones.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Rods** are sensitive to **dim light**; **cones** work in **bright light**.
2. Rods do **not** detect colour and contain **visual purple**; cones **detect colour** and are crowded at the **yellow spot**.

questions.solution_md: Light level; colour; position.

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the vertical section of the human eye. Label the cornea, iris, lens, ciliary body, retina and blind spot.

answer.model_answer_md: A round eyeball with the **cornea** bulging at the front; the **iris** on either side of the pupil; the biconvex **lens** behind it, held by suspensory ligaments from the **ciliary body**; the three-layered wall with the **retina** innermost; the **yellow spot** opposite the lens and the **blind spot** where the optic nerve leaves.

questions.solution_md: Labelled V.S. of the eye.

marking_scheme.step: Front parts: cornea, iris, lens, ciliary body
Wall layers with retina and blind spot

questions.stem_md: When Asha looks up from her phone to a tree far away, her

options.text_md: ciliary muscles contract and her lenses become thicker
ciliary muscles relax and her lenses become thinner
retinas move nearer to the lenses

questions.solution_md: For distant vision the ciliary muscles relax, the ligaments tighten and the lens flattens — option (c).

questions.stem_md: On entering a dark cinema hall from bright sunlight, Vivek sees almost nothing at first, but after a few minutes he can see the seats. This is because

options.text_md: his pupils narrow and his cones become active
his pupils widen and his rods build up visual purple again

questions.solution_md: Adaptation to the dark: the pupil dilates and bleached visual purple in the rods is re-formed — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In bright sunlight the pupil becomes small because

options.text_md: the radial muscles of the iris contract
the circular muscles of the iris contract

questions.solution_md: Contraction of the circular muscles of the iris narrows the pupil, letting in less light — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Stereoscopic vision mainly helps us to

options.text_md: judge depth and the distance of objects

questions.solution_md: Two eyes see a scene from slightly different angles; the brain combines them into a three-dimensional picture — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Threading a needle is much harder with one eye closed, mainly because

options.text_md: the closed eye stops the other from focusing
the pupil of the open eye closes
stereoscopic vision is lost, so it is hard to judge distance

questions.solution_md: With one eye there is no overlap of two views, so depth is hard to judge — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Each human eye can see over about 150° from side to side, and the two eyes together cover about 180°. Over how many degrees do the fields of the two eyes overlap?
questions.solution_md: Overlap $= 150 + 150 - 180 = 120$ degrees: this region is seen by both eyes.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The pupil becomes smaller in bright light.

**Reason (R):** The radial muscles of the iris contract in bright light.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: in bright light the circular muscles contract; radial muscles widen the pupil in dim light — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The lens becomes thinner when we look at a near object.

**Reason (R):** The ciliary muscles contract when we focus on a near object.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: for a near object the lens becomes thicker. The reason is true: contraction of the ciliary muscles slackens the ligaments — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hunting animals such as owls and cats have both eyes facing forward.

**Reason (R):** Overlapping fields of view give stereoscopic vision, which helps to judge distance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and judging the distance of prey is exactly what forward-facing eyes with overlapping fields provide — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The ability of the eye to focus on both near and distant objects by changing the curvature of the lens is called ______.
questions.solution_md: Accommodation.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: on walking from bright sunlight into a dark room, we cannot see clearly at first.

answer.model_answer_md: The **pupil** takes time to **widen**, and the **visual purple** of the rods, bleached by bright light, takes time to **re-form**.

questions.solution_md: Dark adaptation takes time.

marking_scheme.step: Pupil widening and visual purple re-forming take time

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a rabbit, with eyes on the sides of its head, judges distance less well than a human does.

answer.model_answer_md: Its two fields of view **hardly overlap**, so it has little **stereoscopic vision** (though it sees a wider area around it).

questions.solution_md: Little overlap.

marking_scheme.step: Little overlap, so little stereoscopic vision

questions.stem_md: Explain how the eye focuses on a near object.

answer.model_answer_md: The **ciliary muscles contract**, which **slackens the suspensory ligaments**. The elastic lens then becomes **thicker and more convex**, with a **shorter focal length**, so the image of the near object falls on the retina.

questions.solution_md: Ciliary contraction; thicker lens.

marking_scheme.step: Lens thicker, image on the retina

questions.stem_md: Explain how the eye adjusts when you step out of a dark room into bright sunlight.

answer.model_answer_md: The **circular muscles** of the iris contract, so the **pupil narrows** and less light enters. The **visual purple** in the rods is **bleached**, so vision now depends on the **cones**, which work in bright light.

questions.solution_md: Pupil narrows; cones take over.

questions.stem_md: In myopia, the image of a distant object is formed

options.text_md: behind the retina, because the eyeball is too short
on the retina but upside down
in front of the retina, because the eyeball is too long

questions.solution_md: A long eyeball (or a too-curved lens) brings parallel rays to a focus before the retina — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Short-sightedness (myopia) is corrected with spectacles having
questions.solution_md: A concave lens spreads the rays so that the eye focuses them on the retina — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Ritu sees distant objects clearly, but the letters of her book look blurred. The doctor says her eyeball is a little short. She needs

options.text_md: convex lenses, as she has hypermetropia
concave lenses, as she has myopia
cylindrical lenses, as she has astigmatism
an operation to remove the lens, as she has cataract

questions.solution_md: Long-sightedness: near images would form behind the retina; a convex lens corrects it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Mrs Pillai, aged 52, reads her newspaper only when holding it at arm's length, though her distant vision is good. The most likely cause is that

options.text_md: her eyeballs have become too long
her eye lenses have become less elastic with age
her corneas have become unevenly curved
her retinas have lost all their cones

questions.solution_md: Presbyopia: the ageing lens loses elasticity (and the ciliary muscles weaken), so near focusing fails — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Astigmatism is caused by

options.text_md: an uneven curvature of the cornea, and is corrected with cylindrical lenses
a cloudy lens, and is corrected by surgery
a short eyeball, and is corrected with convex lenses
loss of rods, and is corrected with vitamin A

questions.solution_md: An irregularly curved cornea focuses lines in different directions differently; cylindrical lenses correct it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In cataract,

options.text_md: the retina becomes detached and is corrected by spectacles
the eyeball becomes too long and is corrected with concave lenses
the lens becomes cloudy and is replaced by an artificial lens in surgery
the iris stops working and the pupil stays wide

questions.solution_md: Cataract is clouding (opacity) of the lens; surgery replaces it with an artificial lens — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A short-sighted student cannot see clearly beyond 200 cm. His spectacle lens must make distant objects appear to be at this far point. What is the focal length, in cm, of the concave lens he needs? (Give the size only, without a sign.)
questions.solution_md: The focal length of the concave lens equals the far point: 200 cm (written as −200 cm for a concave lens).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A short-sighted person is given spectacles with concave lenses.

**Reason (R):** In myopia, the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and since the rays meet too soon, a diverging (concave) lens is needed to move the image back onto the retina — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hypermetropia is corrected by using concave lenses.
questions.solution_md: False. Hypermetropia is corrected by convex lenses; myopia by concave lenses.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the condition in which the lens of the eye becomes cloudy, causing blurred vision.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cataract.**

questions.solution_md: Cataract.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Myopia, Stereoscopic vision, Astigmatism, Cataract.

answer.model_answer_md: **Stereoscopic vision**; the others are **defects of the eye**.

questions.solution_md: Stereoscopic vision is normal binocular vision.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between myopia and hypermetropia.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Myopia blurs **distant** objects (image **in front of** the retina); hypermetropia blurs **near** objects (image **behind** it).
2. Myopia: eyeball too **long**, corrected by a **concave** lens. Hypermetropia: eyeball too **short**, corrected by a **convex** lens.

questions.solution_md: Image position; eyeball length and lens.

questions.stem_md: State the cause and the correction of presbyopia, astigmatism and cataract.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Presbyopia:** the lens loses **elasticity** with age; corrected with **convex** (or bifocal) lenses.
2. **Astigmatism:** **uneven curvature of the cornea**; corrected with **cylindrical** lenses.
3. **Cataract:** the lens becomes **cloudy**; treated by **surgery** that replaces it with an artificial lens.

questions.solution_md: Cause and correction of each.

(b) A **concave lens** in front of the eye **diverges** the rays slightly, so that after passing through the eye lens they meet **on the retina**.

questions.solution_md: Stapes (stirrup).

questions.solution_md: Equalises pressure.

answer.model_answer_md: The **pinna** and auditory canal ending at the **tympanum**; the middle ear with the three **ossicles** in a chain from the tympanum to the oval window and the **Eustachian tube** running down; the inner ear with the **vestibule**, three **semicircular canals** and the coiled **cochlea**, with the auditory nerve.

questions.solution_md: Fluid moving in the semicircular canals stimulates sensory hairs, signalling rotation — option (d).

questions.stem_md: State the role of the semicircular canals and of the vestibule in keeping our balance.

answer.model_answer_md: The **semicircular canals** detect **movement and rotation** of the head, as their fluid moves and bends sensory hairs. The **vestibule** detects the **position of the head** with respect to **gravity** when we are still (static balance).

questions.solution_md: Movement; position.

questions.stem_md: Trace the path of a sound from the pinna to the brain.

answer.model_answer_md: The **pinna** collects sound waves and directs them along the **auditory canal** to the **tympanum**, which vibrates. The **malleus, incus and stapes** pass the vibrations to the **oval window** and into the fluid of the **cochlea**, where sensory hair cells produce impulses. The **auditory nerve** carries these to the **brain** (cerebrum), where the sound is perceived.

questions.solution_md: Pinna to brain.

questions.passage_md: Rahul, a Class 10 student, can read his textbook easily but cannot read the blackboard from the back bench. The optometrist finds that his eyeballs are slightly longer than normal and that he cannot see clearly beyond 200 cm. His grandfather, on the other hand, sees distant objects well but needs spectacles to read.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Myopia** (short-sightedness).

**(b)** It forms **in front of the retina**. Because his eyeball is **too long**, the parallel rays from the distant board meet **before** they reach the retina, so the image on the retina is blurred.

**(c)** 200 cm

**(d)** (i) (a) A long eyeball with parallel rays meeting **in front of the retina**. (b) A **concave lens** before the eye making the rays **diverge** slightly, so that they meet **on the retina**.

**OR** (ii) A concave lens **diverges** the parallel rays from the board so that they seem to come from a point within his **far point**. His eye lens can focus such rays, so the image now falls **on the retina** instead of in front of it, and the board looks **sharp**.

**(e)** He has **presbyopia**. With age the **lens loses its elasticity** and the **ciliary muscles weaken**, so the lens cannot become thick enough to focus **near objects**. It is corrected with **convex** (reading or bifocal) lenses.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Myopia.

**(b)** In front of the retina.

**(c)** It equals his far point: 200 cm.

**(d)** (i) Two ray diagrams.

(ii) Diverges rays; image moves onto the retina.

**(e)** Presbyopia; convex lenses.

questions.stem_md: Read the following and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md: Neha walked from the bright afternoon sun into a dark cinema hall. For a minute she could hardly see the steps; then she began to make out the seats and the people in them. When she came out after the film, she screwed up her eyes against the glare.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** They became **larger** (dilated).

**(b)** In dim light the **radial muscles** of the iris **contract** (and the circular muscles relax), pulling the iris outwards so the **pupil widens** and lets in **more light**.

**(c)** The **rods**. Their **visual purple** had been **bleached** by bright sunlight and had to be **re-formed** (using vitamin A) before they could respond to dim light.

**(d)** Her pupils were still **wide**, so **too much light** entered and dazzled her. Screwing up the eyes cut down the light until the **pupils narrowed** by contraction of the **circular muscles**.

**(e)** 1. Rods work in **dim light**; cones in **bright light**.
2. Rods do **not detect colour**; cones **do**.
3. Rods contain **visual purple** and are spread over most of the retina; cones are crowded at the **yellow spot**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Dilated.

**(b)** Radial muscles contract.

**(c)** Rods; visual purple re-forms.

**(d)** Pupils still wide.

**(e)** Light, colour, pigment and position.

answer.model_answer_md: They became **larger** (dilated).

children.stem_md: Which cells allowed Neha to see in the dark hall, and why did they take time to work?

answer.model_answer_md: The **rods**. Their **visual purple** had been **bleached** by bright sunlight and had to be **re-formed** (using vitamin A) before they could respond to dim light.

answer.model_answer_md: Her pupils were still **wide**, so **too much light** entered and dazzled her. Screwing up the eyes cut down the light until the **pupils narrowed** by contraction of the **circular muscles**.

children.stem_md: State three differences between rods and cones.
